doc.title: Jimmy Heath interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, September 8, 2014

title: Jazz as African-American music and the 'white man's music' claim
summary: Heath says white players claim jazz though African-Americans created it, and notes players worldwide absorb its improvisational language.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You said something, just in what you said about the blues makes me wonder — you were talking about how jazz is sometimes now thought of as the “white man’s music.” And what is the reason for that?
I didn’t say it was the white man’s music. I said the white man is claiming it for his music —

— but it was created by African-Americans. And there were a few whites, even at that time, you know, Bix Beiderbecke and people back there, they were in that same mode. But the majority of the performers were African-Americans. Now all over the world there are people — you know I’ve been all over and I hear people playing like Sonny Rollins or Coltrane or Dizzy or whoever, from here, coming from all over the world. They’ve heard that music and they’ve absorbed some of the improvisational language.
